thread: I keep reviewing AI agent prompts, and the gap keeps coming back: the guardrails were never written down. So I built CrewScore ({package_version}). It checks agent instructions against {concept_count} public controls across {dimension_count} dimensions — browser or CI. https://crewscore.ai

What it found on a public corpus of {total_prompts} prompts ({production_n} production-labeled): median written-control coverage {production_median}/100. Coverage, not a safety grade — the number says which controls the text is missing, not whether the agent behaves.

Try it: paste instructions at crewscore.ai (your text never leaves the browser), or run `crewscore scan .` in CI with the GitHub Action. Missing controls show up as explainable findings with suggested wording you review. pip install crewscore

What CrewScore is not: not a certification, not a red team, not a quality ranking, not proof of runtime behavior. Every rule, regex, and the validation corpus are public: https://github.com/shmindmaster/crewscore — built and maintained by me; Pendoah is my company context.

linkedin.text:
Would you let an AI assistant serve your customers without written rules?

Most AI assistants run on a block of written instructions. When I checked {total_prompts} publicly available prompts — {production_n} of them from production tools — the median written-guardrail coverage was {production_median} out of 100. Not because teams are careless. Because nobody checks whether the rules got written down.

So I built CrewScore ({package_version}). You give it your assistant's instructions, and it checks them against {concept_count} common guardrails: does a big action need human approval? does it stop when it is unsure? does it cite sources? is there a cap on cost? It runs locally in your browser — your text is never uploaded. For coding-agent config files it reports configuration-smell findings only.

What it deliberately does not do matters as much. It does not certify safety, and it cannot prove the AI will behave. It shows you which safeguards you forgot to write down. Written rules are step one — testing and human oversight are still yours.

Try it free: https://crewscore.ai
Open source for teams: pip install crewscore

{created_by} {operating_context}

answer_bank.question: What does CrewScore measure?
answer_bank.answer: CrewScore measures whether the prompt text states controls across {dimension_count} dimensions and {concept_count} published controls. The score is structural text coverage, not runtime behavior.

answer_bank.question: How does it stay honest?
answer_bank.answer: It uses deterministic regex over local text and writes every number from current rules and corpus evidence in one repository-trusted path.

answer_bank.question: Does CrewScore certify compliance or safety?
answer_bank.answer: No. It does not certify compliance, does not provide a runtime safety guarantee, or replace legal review. It only reports what your prompt text says.
